meaning: Root, major third and fifth. A root with no quality word, and the spellings maj, M and major, all name it.
Root, minor third and fifth. An m or a dash right after the root marks it.
Root, major second and fifth, with no third. The second takes the place of the third.
Root, fourth and fifth, with no third. A bare sus after the root means this chord, not sus2.
Root and fifth with no third, optionally with the octave on top. It is neither major nor minor.
A major triad plus a minor seventh. A bare dom after the root also means the seventh chord.
A major triad plus a major seventh. The triangle and caret signs name the major-seventh family, and maj with no number means the triad.
A minor triad plus a minor seventh. A dash before the 7 reads as minor.
A major triad plus the ninth, with no seventh.
A dominant seventh plus the ninth. A bare 9 implies the seventh below it.
A major seventh plus the ninth.
A minor seventh plus the ninth.
A chord over a named bass note, written chord/bass. The bass is the lowest sounding pitch and differs from the root.
Root, minor third and diminished fifth. The signs o and ° after the root also write it.
A diminished triad plus a minor seventh, also called minor seven flat five. The signs ø and h write it.
A diminished triad plus a diminished seventh, nine semitones above the root. The sign o7 writes it.
A major triad plus a major sixth, with no seventh. A 6 after the root cancels an implied seventh.
Root, major third and raised fifth. A plus sign right after the root, with no number, means this chord.
A minor triad plus a major sixth.
A sixth chord plus the ninth, with no seventh.
A minor sixth chord plus the ninth.
A minor triad plus a major seventh. The M after an m marks the major seventh.
An augmented triad plus a minor seventh. A plus sign beside the 7 writes it.
A suspended fourth plus a minor seventh.
A dominant seventh plus a flat ninth, 13 semitones above the root.
A dominant seventh plus a sharp ninth, 15 semitones above the root.
A minor triad plus the ninth, with no seventh.
A major triad plus the eleventh, 17 semitones above the root, with no seventh. A bare 4 is ambiguous: prefer asking, or write sus4.
Root, third, fifth, minor seventh, ninth and eleventh, the textbook stack. Voicings usually leave out the third, which clashes with the eleventh a ninth above it.
A minor seventh plus the ninth and eleventh.
A dominant seventh plus the ninth and thirteenth, with the eleventh left out.
A major seventh plus the ninth and thirteenth, with the eleventh left out.
A minor seventh plus the ninth and thirteenth, with the eleventh left out.
A suspended fourth plus a minor seventh and the ninth.
A major seventh plus a raised eleventh, 18 semitones above the root.

Root, major third and minor seventh, plus at least two of the flat ninth, sharp ninth, sharp eleventh and flat thirteenth. The natural 5th, 9th, 11th and 13th stay out; the usual default is 0 4 10 15 20.
Three or four tones stacked in fourths: root, fourth and minor seventh, with an optional minor tenth (15 semitones).
Two triads sounding together, one above the other. A slash followed by a whole triad name writes it, while a slash and one note is a bass note.
An augmented triad plus a major seventh.
A dominant seventh with the fifth lowered to the tritone, six semitones above the root.
A minor-major seventh plus the ninth.
A dominant seventh plus a raised eleventh, 18 semitones above the root, with the fifth kept.
A dominant seventh plus a flat thirteenth, 20 semitones above the root.
A major seventh plus the ninth and eleventh, the textbook stack. As with the dominant 11, voicings usually leave out the third, which clashes with the eleventh.
A dominant seventh with alterations: add each altered tone and drop the natural tone it replaces. Write the alterations in parentheses, such as b9 and #11.
Tones stacked in fifths: root, fifth and ninth, with an optional thirteenth (21 semitones).
Three or more tones packed in adjacent steps, either chromatic as 0 1 2 or diatonic as 0 2 4.
